content: Rumors Stats Odds Betting Newsletter LOCAL Brevard County health officials warn of rabies, West Nile risks Jim Waymer Florida Today Sept. 3, 2026, 12:06 p.m. ET Health officials in Brevard County, Florida, have issued warnings for both West Nile virus and rabies. A rabies alert was issued after a raccoon captured in Melbourne tested positive for the virus. Officials advise residents to avoid wild animals, secure pets, and take precautions against mosquito bites. Florida health officials warned Thursday about risks to Brevard County residents from rabies and the West Nile virus. Several sentinel chickens within the county have recently tested positive for West Nile virus, triggering a health advisory. Thursday's rabies alert was in response to a confirmed case of rabies in a raccoon that was captured in the Melbourne area off Andrews Avenue on Aug. 27. State health officials and Brevard County Mosquito Control are coordinating surveillance and prevention efforts "by enhanced monitoring for mosquitoes and diseases as well as targeted mosquito treatment and overnight spraying to reduce the risk of disease transmission," FDOH said in a release. State and county officials continue to conduct statewide surveillance for mosquito-borne illnesses,including West Nile virus infections, Eastern equine encephalitis, St. Louis encephalitis, malaria,chikungunya and dengue. Health officials urge the public to avoid being bitten by mosquitoes by taking basic precautions, such as avoiding being outdoors at dawn and dusk, using mosquito repellants and/or wearing long-sleaves and pants to cover the skin. Residents also are encouraged to report dead birds to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission’s website: myfwc.com/research/wildlife/health/avian. Brevard health officials issue Sept. 3 rabies alert On Thursday (Sept. 3) state health officials issued a rabies alert in Brevard in response to a confirmed case of the viral infection in a raccoon that was captured in the Melbourne area off Andrews Avenue on Aug. 27. "People and domestic animals should always avoid physical contact with wild animals," Florida health officials warned in a press release. That includes raccoons, bats, foxes, skunks, otters, bobcats, coyotes, which carry a higher risk of human exposure and a need for rabies post-exposure treatment. "If you are exposed to rabies, receiving appropriate treatment after exposure will protect you from the risk of rabies." The rabies alert is for 60 days and includes the following boundaries in Brevard County: Northern boundary: West Eau Gallie Boulevard Southern boundary: Sarno Road Eastern boundary: Croton Road Western boundary: North Wickham Road Immunize your pets and livestock based on your veterinarian’s recommended schedule. Take the following precautions to prevent rabies exposure: According to Florida Department of Health: Keep pets under direct supervision and on a leash, and keep livestock secured on your property. If an animal bites your pet or livestock, seek veterinary assistance for the animal immediately and contact Brevard County Sherrif’s Office Animal Services at 321-633-2024. Avoid contact with wild or stray animals. Do not handle, feed, or unintentionally attract them with outdoor pet food, open garbage cans, or other sources of food. If you have been bitten or scratched by a wild or domestic animal, seek medical attention, and report the injury to DOH-Brevard by calling 321-634-6337 option 3. Never adopt wild animals or bring them into your home; instead, contact a licensed wildlife rehabilitator. Prevent wildlife, including bats, from entering living quarters or occupied spaces in homes, schools, and other similar areas where they might come in contact with people and pets. For information on rabies, please visit FloridaHealth.gov/Rabies or contact DOH-Brevard at 321-634-6337 option 3. Contact Waymer at jwaymer@floridatoday.com. Featured Weekly Ad

content: Local Sports High School Huddle Scene Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTH Possible rabies exposure in 7 NC counties after baby goats test positive Iris Seaton Asheville Citizen Times Sept. 1, 2026, 2:19 p.m. ET Rabies was confirmed in three baby goats from a North Carolina mobile petting zoo. The goats were potentially exposed to rabies by a skunk in late July. Anyone who had contact with the goats between July 28 and Aug. 27 may have been exposed. The infected animals were taken to events in at least seven North Carolina counties. Rabies was detected in three baby goats which were in contact with many North Carolina residents through a mobile petting zoo, the N.C. Department of Health and Human Services warned. According to a Friday, Aug. 28 release, the N.C. DHHS and N.C. Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services were first notified of a potential rabies exposure among four baby goats at Farm Adventures in Harmony on Aug. 27. The goats are believed to have been exposed to rabies by a skunk that entered a pen where they were kept in late July. The N.C. State Laboratory of Public Health confirmed rabies in three of the baby goats on Aug. 28. The fourth goat was not tested but is also assumed to have been infected. Officials are working with the farm and impacted local health departments to gather information about potential exposure dates and locations; based on information gathered Aug. 28, it has been determined that no other animals on the farm pose a rabies risk. The infected animals were taken to at least seven NC counties according to latest information from NC agencies. Here's what else to know. Where was rabies detected in North Carolina? Baby goat exposure locations Farm Adventures operates a petting zoo in Harmony, as well as off-site mobile petting zoo events. Anyone who had contact with the baby goats at any location between July 28 and Aug. 27 may have been exposed while the animals were infectious. Impacted individuals should contact their local health department to determine whether medications are needed to prevent infection, and are encouraged to call before visiting an emergency department or urgent care clinic to determine if treatment is needed and where it can be accessed. Known exposure locations where the infected baby goats were taken include: Jurney's Assisted Living, 1942 Van Haven Drive, Statesville, Iredell County - July 28 Private event, Mecklenburg County - July 30 Community Connections Back-to-School Bash, Breeden Amphitheater, 333 S. Main St., Lexington, Davidson County - Aug. 1 Brookdale Peachtree, 2806 Peachtree Road, Statesville, Iredell County - Aug. 6 Private event, Watauga County - Aug. 8 Private event in Burke County - Aug. 9 Masonic Picnic Grounds, 201 Poplar St., Mocksville, Davie County - Aug. 15 Private event, Durham County - Aug. 16 Private event, Iredell County - Aug. 22 Private, Durham County - Aug. 23 Public health officials are working with event organizers to notify attendees who may have had contact with the goats. The investigation is ongoing, with additional information about potential exposure locations to be released when available. Have there been any human rabies cases in North Carolina? The N.C. DHHS statement noted that human rabies infections are "extremely rare" in the U.S., and no human cases have been reported in the state since 2011. How is rabies spread? The N.C. DHHS states that rabies can be spread from wild animals to pets and people primarily through bites, scratches, or infected saliva touching broken skin or mucous membranes. In the case of the infected baby goats, it is possible that people could have been exposed to the virus through saliva from an infected animal. As baby goats are often bottle-fed, handled closely or cuddled, public health officials are "working proactively" to ensure anyone who had direct contact with the affected animals is evaluated. What animals can carry rabies? Though any mammal can carry and spread rabies, Mayo Clinic states that pets and farm most likely to transmit the rabies virus include cats, cows, dogs, ferrets, goats and horses. Wild animals most likely to spread the virus include bats, beavers, coyotes, foxes, monkeys, raccoons, skunks and woodchucks. What are the symptoms of rabies in animals? Humans? Rabies is almost always fatal in mammals, including humans, unless the proper medications are given before symptoms develop. Symptoms can begin weeks to months after someone is exposed. Once the virus enters the body, it travels along the nerves to the brain. Animals with rabies may show a variety of signs. The American Veterinary Medical Association lists the following symptoms as common: Fearfulness Aggression Excessive drooling Difficulty swallowing Staggering Paralysis Seizures Depression, self-mutilation or increased sensitivity to light in horses and livestock Aggressive behavior or unusually affectionate, friendly or fearless behavior Generally unusual behavior, such as nocturnal animals becoming active during the daytime In humans, early symptoms can be flu-like, including weakness, fever or headache as well as a prickling or itching sensation where someone was bitten or exposed. A full list of rabies symptoms among humans from Mayo Clinic includes: Fever Headache Nausea Vomiting Agitation Anxiety Confusion Hyperactivity Difficulty swallowing Excessive salivation Fear brought on by attempts to drink fluids because of difficulty swallowing water Fear brought on by air blown on the face Hallucinations Insomnia Partial paralysis Iris Seaton is the trending news reporter for the Asheville Citizen Times, part of the USA TODAY Network. Reach her at iseaton@citizentimes.com. Featured Weekly Ad
